I am a 70-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have been farming this land for over 50 years. I went to school longer than most of my peers, and I have always paid close attention to what the agricultural extension agents and researchers from the China Agricultural University station here in Quzhou recommend — though I do not follow everything blindly. I know my own soil and microclimate.

It is early spring now, and my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October. I always plant winter wheat and follow it with summer maize; this is the classic *wheat-maize* double-cropping system that makes the most of the North China Plain's heat and water. At my age, I manage **5 mu** total by myself, with some help from my son during harvest and planting rushes. I will not expand because I cannot manage more physically, and I will not shrink because this is the right size to support my household and leave a little surplus to sell.

For the **winter wheat** that is currently greening up: I sowed an **improved variety** — not the newest hybrid, but a proven local improved cultivar that stands up well to the spring winds we get here. I will top-dress nitrogen at green-up and again at jointing, for a total of about **14 kg N per mu**; I will also apply **5 kg P per mu** and **5 kg K per mu** based on soil tests I had done two years ago. The wheat will need **3 irrigations** this season: one at green-up (now), one at jointing, and one at grain filling if the spring turns dry, which it usually does. I will do **2 pesticide applications** — a herbicide in early spring and a fungicide/insecticide mix at heading if I see aphid pressure. I tilled with a **rotary tiller** before autumn sowing, so the soil is already prepared. I expect about **550 kg per mu** if the weather cooperates.

For **summer maize**, which I will plant immediately after wheat harvest in early June: I will use a **hybrid** seed, the same one I have used for three years now because it matures quickly and resists lodging. I will apply **15 kg N per mu**, **4 kg P per mu**, and **5 kg K per mu**, split between basal and a top-dress at the large trumpet stage. Maize here usually needs **2 irrigations** — one at sowing if the soil is too dry after wheat harvest, and one critical irrigation at the large trumpet stage. I will spray **2 times** for weed and pest control. I will use **no-tillage** direct seeding into the wheat stubble; this saves time, fuel, and water, and I have seen it work well on my fields. I expect **650 kg per mu** from the maize.

Why this plan? Because at 70, I need reliability over experimentation. The wheat-maize rotation is what this land and climate are built for. I use enough fertilizer to maintain yields but not so much that I waste money or damage the soil — my education taught me to read the recommendations and adjust them. No-tillage for maize saves my back and my diesel. I will not gamble on new cash crops like vegetables because the labor and market risk are too high for me now.
